title: Who Ruled Judaea?
sub: Grades 5–8 · Social Studies · Coins as primary sources
objective: Students will use coins as primary sources to describe how power was layered in New Testament Judaea: an **emperor** in Rome, **local rulers from Herod’s family**, and **Roman governors**, with an independent **neighboring king** across the border. They will read what a coin’s design reveals about its maker and its audience, and practice **corroboration** — checking one source against independent evidence — using the Pilate stone, Josephus and Suetonius.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: No single person ruled Judaea in Jesus’ lifetime. Coins show us who held power, and checking one source against another is how historians decide what to trust.

items.text: read a coin as a primary source: who made it, for whom, and what its design reveals

materials: The *Who ruled when* chart on page 3, projected or printed
Luke 23:6–12 and Acts 25:10–12, in Bibles or projected; the Gospel Timeline on a screen if you have one
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** the cases run in order — the rulers of the Nativity in Case 6, of the trial in Case 7, of the apostles in Case 8. At each case, have students name each coin’s level of power. Online, the Gospel Timeline sets all eleven coins beside their passages.

steps.title: A face, and no face
script: Show the Tribute Penny beside Pilate’s prutah. Both were in people’s hands in Judaea in Jesus’ lifetime. *“One shows a man’s face. The other shows a ladle and three ears of grain. Who made each one — and why would they choose such different pictures?”* Take guesses, then: *“Coins are messages from the people in charge. Today we use them to find out who was in charge.”*

steps.purpose: Start reading coins as messages from the people in charge.
students: One coin shows a face, one a ladle. Who made each one?
Why would they choose such different pictures?

steps.title: Four kinds of power
script: Walk through the four kinds of ruler on the chart (page 3), showing each coin.

groups.label: The emperor in Rome
groups.text: Ruled the whole Roman Empire from Rome. Augustus never visited Judaea, yet his census sent Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem.

groups.text: Aretas IV ruled the Nabataean Kingdom, east of Judaea. When Antipas divorced his daughter, Aretas went to war against him.

steps.purpose: Set out the four layers of power the coins reveal, and who sat at the top.
students: Name one ruler of each kind.
Who did a Roman governor answer to?

steps.title: Who answered to whom?
script: Then show the layers at work: Pilate sent Jesus to Antipas because Jesus was from Galilee, Antipas’s territory (Luke 23:6–12); Paul, a Roman citizen, went over the governor’s head — *“I appeal to Caesar!”* (Acts 25:10–12). Ask: *who answered to whom?*

verse.text: Paul answered: ‘I am now standing before Caesar’s court, where I ought to be tried. I have not done any wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know very well. I appeal to Caesar!’ After Festus had conferred with his advisers, he declared: ‘You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!’

screen.alt: Paul, standing in a gray robe, makes his case to three seated rulers in a Roman hall; painted by Vasily Surikov

steps.purpose: See the layers of power at work in two trials.
students: Pilate sent Jesus to Herod Antipas. Why him?
Paul went over the governor’s head. To whom?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three levels work from the same rulers and the same coins.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Sort nine rulers by their coins into emperor, Herod’s family, Roman governor or neighboring king; complete a guided timeline; answer *who would you be sent to?*

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Analyze Herod’s and Pilate’s prutahs as primary sources. Complete the ruler chart, then explain what the trials of Jesus and Paul show about layered power.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Test three New Testament claims against coins, the Pilate stone, Josephus and Suetonius. Then argue what coins can prove about the past, and what they cannot.

steps.purpose: Practice reading coins as sources at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three levels work from the same rulers and the same coins.

steps.title: Who ruled when
script: Each group places one ruler on the chart and gives its clue. Then ask: *a coin shows who claimed power — how can we check what the Gospels and Acts say about these rulers?* Let Red-level students answer.

screen.caption: Who ruled when: every ruler with a coin in the exhibition, in the order the exhibition shows them

steps.purpose: Pull the lesson together on one chart, then ask how a claim can be checked.
students: Place one ruler: his kind of power, and his coin’s clue.
How could we check what the Gospels and Acts say about him?

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
